en: Anxiety or fear that something bad will happen; also, understanding or arrest
hook: APPREHENSION: feeling like you're about to be APPREHENDED (arrested).
story: Apprehension. The night before her first viva, Mitu could not sleep. She kept imagining the examiners frowning, a question she could not answer, her voice cracking. By morning her hands were cold and her stomach was tight. That uneasy dread about what might go wrong is apprehension: anxiety or fear that something bad will happen. The word has two other senses: understanding, and the arrest of a criminal. Think of the mind grasping a danger before it arrives. Synonyms: dread, unease.

gre.s: Although the villagers greeted the new dam with ____, fearing floods and lost farmland, their worries proved unfounded when the first monsoon passed without incident.
gre.clue: fearing floods and lost farmland

en: Very enthusiastic or passionate
hook: ARDENT: burning with ARDOR.
story: Ardent. Every Friday at dawn, Rafi's grandfather walks two kilometres to the field where the village boys play cricket. He has not missed a match in thirty years. He knows every player's batting average and shouts advice from the boundary until he is hoarse. He is an ardent fan: passionate and intensely devoted. Ardent comes from the Latin word for burning, the same root as arson. An ardent supporter burns with enthusiasm. Synonyms: fervent, zealous, passionate.

gre.s: Even her most ____ admirers, who had defended every one of her earlier films against hostile reviewers, conceded that her latest effort was a disappointment.
gre.clue: who had defended every one of her earlier films

en: Self-evident; accepted as true without proof
hook: AXIOM: a basic truth in math, needing no proof.
story: Axiomatic. In his first geometry class at university, Tanvir watched the professor write on the board: a straight line can be drawn between any two points. Tanvir raised his hand and asked for the proof. The professor smiled. 'There is none. We simply accept it, because it is obvious.' Such a statement is an axiom, and anything treated this way is axiomatic: self-evident, accepted as true without proof. In economics, it is almost axiomatic that people respond to incentives.

gre.s: It was once considered ____ that the sun revolved around the earth, a truth so plain that no one thought to question it, yet the assumption proved entirely false.
gre.clue: so plain that no one thought to question it

en: To come to an end; to stop
hook: CEASE: CEASE-FIRE, stop shooting.
story: Cease. For three days, construction drills roared outside the hostel from dawn to midnight, and students could not study for their exams. Finally the city authorities issued an order: all work must cease after eight in the evening. That night, at exactly eight, the noise stopped, and the whole hostel cheered. To cease is to come to an end, or to bring something to an end. A ceasefire is when guns stop firing. Something that never stops is unceasing. Synonyms: stop, halt.

gre.s: The two factions agreed to ____ hostilities during the festival, but the fragile truce collapsed only days after the celebrations ended.
gre.clue: the fragile truce

en: Making a certain outcome likely; helpful
hook: CONDUCIVE: CONDUCTS you toward a result.
story: Conducive. Sara could never study in her family's crowded flat in Mirpur, with the television blaring and cousins dropping by. So she found a corner of the university library: soft light, a big window, total silence. In that corner she finished two chapters in one afternoon. The library was conducive to study: it made good work likely. Conducive means making a certain outcome likely, or helpful to it, and it is usually followed by to. Think: it conducts you toward a result.

gre.s: Critics argued that the open-plan office, with its constant chatter and interruptions, was hardly ____ to the deep concentration that serious research demands.
gre.clue: with its constant chatter and interruptions

en: Relating to the physical body; material rather than spiritual
hook: CORPOREAL: CORPS, CORPSE, body.
story: Corporeal. Grandmother Rahima tells the village children about ghosts who walk through walls and leave no footprints. Her grandson Babu, a physics student, laughs: a ghost could never open a door, he says, because it has no body. Ghosts and spirits are imagined as non-physical. Humans, with hunger, bruises and tired feet, are corporeal: relating to the physical body, material rather than spiritual. Corpus is Latin for body, as in corpse and corps. The opposite is incorporeal.

gre.s: The monks believed that ____ pleasures such as food and comfort were mere distractions; only by disciplining the body could they attend to the needs of the soul.
gre.clue: only by disciplining the body

en: Rigidly applying a theory without regard for practical considerations
hook: DOCTRINAIRE: follows the DOCTRINE no matter what.
story: Doctrinaire. A new manager at a garment factory near Dhaka had read one textbook on efficiency and believed every word. When workers explained that his new shift schedule ignored the monsoon flooding on their roads, he refused to change a single line, because the theory said so. Production collapsed. His approach was doctrinaire: rigidly applying a theory without regard for practical reality. The word comes from doctrine, a fixed set of beliefs. Opposite: pragmatic. Synonyms: dogmatic, inflexible.

gre.s: Unlike her ____ predecessor, who insisted on following party ideology even when it produced obvious failures, the new minister was willing to adapt policies to local conditions.
gre.clue: insisted on following party ideology even when it produced obvious failures

en: Drawing from a wide variety of sources or styles
hook: ECLECTIC: ELECTS a bit from everywhere.
story: Eclectic. Joya's playlist confuses her friends. Rabindra Sangeet is followed by Korean pop, then a Bach cello suite, then a baul song from Kushtia, then American jazz. Her bookshelf is the same: poetry, physics, cookbooks and detective novels side by side. Her taste is eclectic: drawn from a wide variety of sources and styles. The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to pick out, so an eclectic person selects the best from everywhere. Synonyms: diverse, wide-ranging.

gre.s: The architect's style resists easy categorization: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction, it is thoroughly ____.
gre.clue: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction

en: Mental calmness and composure, especially in difficulty
hook: EQUA-NIMITY: an EQUAL, balanced mind.
story: Equanimity. The power went out in the middle of Arif's online job interview. His laptop died, the generator failed, and he had to rejoin on his phone from the stairwell, fifteen minutes late. Instead of panicking, he apologised calmly, smiled, and answered every question clearly. The interviewers were impressed by his equanimity: mental calmness and composure, especially in difficulty. Equi means equal and animus means mind, so equanimity is an even mind. Synonyms: composure, poise, calm.

gre.s: Though her colleagues panicked when the funding was suddenly withdrawn, the director responded with remarkable ____, calmly drafting a new budget that same afternoon.
gre.clue: calmly drafting a new budget that same afternoon

en: Unreasonably high, especially of price
hook: EX-ORBIT-ANT: prices gone OUT OF ORBIT.
story: Exorbitant. The night before Eid, Imran went to buy a bus ticket home to Rangpur. The usual fare was eight hundred taka. The man at the counter demanded three thousand. Rickshaw fares had tripled, and even a cup of tea cost double. 'These prices are exorbitant,' Imran groaned: unreasonably high. Ex means out of, and orbit means track, so an exorbitant price has wandered right out of its normal orbit. Synonyms: excessive, extortionate, outrageous.

gre.s: Many families who once used the private clinic now avoid it, since its ____ fees put even routine checkups beyond the reach of ordinary workers.
gre.clue: put even routine checkups beyond the reach of ordinary workers

en: Changing frequently, especially in loyalty or affection
hook: FICKLE: FLICKERS like a candle.
story: Fickle. Last year the whole neighbourhood adored a young cricketer. Posters of him hung in every tea stall. Then he scored zero in two matches, and overnight the same fans tore down his posters and cheered a new hero. Public affection is fickle: changing frequently, especially in loyalty or affection. Dhaka's weather in April is fickle too, sunny one hour and stormy the next. Contrast with steadfast, which means firmly loyal. Synonyms: capricious, inconstant.

gre.s: Politicians who rely on the ____ support of voters soon learn that a single unpopular decision can turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents.
gre.clue: turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents

en: Not literal; using figures of speech like metaphors
hook: FIGURATIVE: a FIGURE of speech.
story: Figurative. When Shuvo's mother said he had a mountain of homework, his little sister ran to the window looking for the mountain. She took the phrase literally. But their mother was speaking in a figurative way: not literal, using a figure of speech. Metaphors, similes and exaggerations are all figurative language. Telling an actor to break a leg is figurative; nobody wants an actual broken leg. The opposite of figurative is literal. Synonyms: metaphorical, symbolic.

gre.s: Readers who interpret the poet's 'burning city' as an actual fire miss the point; the phrase is ____, describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze.
gre.clue: describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze

en: Agitated, nervous, and confused
hook: FLUSTERED: FLUSHED and FLUTTERED.
story: Flustered. Lamia had rehearsed her presentation twenty times. But on the day, the projector would not connect, her notes slid onto the floor, and the professor said, 'We are short of time, please hurry.' Her cheeks went hot, she mixed up two slides, and she forgot her own opening line. She was flustered: agitated, nervous and confused. Fluster sounds like flutter, the way a frightened bird's wings flap about. Opposite: composed, unruffled. Synonyms: rattled, frazzled.

gre.s: Though normally unflappable in debate, the senator became visibly ____ when a reporter produced the documents, stammering and contradicting his own earlier statements.
gre.clue: stammering and contradicting his own earlier statements

en: Easily deceived or tricked
hook: GULLIBLE: like a sea GULL that swallows anything thrown at it.
story: Gullible. A text message arrived on Kamal's uncle's phone: 'Congratulations! You have won fifty lakh taka in a lottery. Send two thousand taka to claim your prize.' He had never bought a lottery ticket, yet he sent the money at once. Of course, there was no prize. He was gullible: easily deceived or tricked. Picture a hungry gull, a seabird that swallows anything thrown to it. Scammers hunt for gullible victims. Synonyms: credulous, naive.

gre.s: Far from being ____, the investigator questioned every claim the witness made, insisting on documents for even the most trivial details.
gre.clue: questioned every claim the witness made

en: Peculiar to an individual; distinctive and unusual
hook: IDIO-SYNCRATIC: IDIO means one's own (as in idiom).
story: Idiosyncratic. Professor Haque always lectures barefoot, writes on the board only with his left hand, and opens every class by singing a line from Lalon. His students imitate him affectionately. His habits are idiosyncratic: peculiar to him alone, distinctive and unusual. Idios is Greek for one's own, the same root as idiom. An idiosyncrasy is one such personal quirk. An idiosyncratic writing style is instantly recognisable as one person's. Synonyms: quirky, eccentric, peculiar.

gre.s: The novelist's spelling and punctuation are so ____ that editors hesitate to correct them, fearing they would erase the very quirks that make her voice unmistakable.
gre.clue: the very quirks that make her voice unmistakable

en: Happening as a minor part or consequence of something more important
hook: INCIDENTAL: just a side INCIDENT.
story: Incidental. Ishita joined the photography club only to learn how to use her new camera. But on the club's trips she made five close friends and discovered a love of travel. Those friendships were incidental benefits: they came along as minor side effects of her main purpose. Incidental means happening as a minor part or consequence of something more important. Incidental expenses are small extra costs, like rickshaw fares on a business trip. Contrast with essential or central.

gre.s: The lawyer argued that the photograph was merely ____ to the case, a minor detail that had no bearing on the central question of who signed the contract.
gre.clue: a minor detail that had no bearing on the central question

en: Firmly fixed or established, hard to change
hook: INGRAINED: deep IN the GRAIN of the wood.
story: Ingrained. Rahim moved from his village to a modern Dhaka office where everyone drank coffee and spoke English in meetings. Yet ten years later he still woke at dawn without an alarm, still removed his shoes at every door, and still touched the feet of elders. These habits were ingrained: firmly fixed and hard to change. Picture a stain worked so deep into the grain of wood that no scrubbing can remove it. Synonyms: deep-rooted, entrenched.

gre.s: Prejudices that are ____ in a culture rarely vanish with the passage of a single law; they persist for generations, handed down quietly from parents to children.
gre.clue: they persist for generations

en: Boldly rude and disrespectful
hook: INSOLENT: INSULTING.
story: Insolent. When the headmaster asked Sabbir why he was late again, Sabbir leaned back, chewed his gum loudly, and said, 'Why do you care? It is not your life.' The whole class gasped. Nobody spoke to the headmaster like that. Sabbir's reply was insolent: boldly rude and disrespectful, especially toward someone in authority. Contrast it with deferential, which means politely respectful. Insolent and impudent are close cousins. Synonyms: impertinent, cheeky, brazen.

gre.s: The new recruit's ____ remarks to the general, delivered with a smirk in front of the entire regiment, earned him a week of confinement to barracks.
gre.clue: delivered with a smirk in front of the entire regiment

en: To mock or ridicule through satire
hook: LAMPOON: like a cartoon that LAMPS (lights up) someone's flaws for laughs.
story: Lampoon. Every winter, Dhaka University students stage a comedy night. This year one sketch showed a minister promising smooth new roads while standing knee-deep in a flooded street, still smiling for the cameras. The audience howled. The students lampooned the minister: they mocked him through satire. Lampoon is also a noun, meaning a piece of writing or performance that ridicules someone. Cartoonists lampoon politicians every day. Synonyms: satirize, parody, ridicule.

gre.s: Rather than attack the dictator directly, the playwright chose to ____ him, exaggerating his vanity until audiences could not stop laughing.
gre.clue: exaggerating his vanity until audiences could not stop laughing

en: Rich, elaborate, and generous; to give generously
hook: LAVISH: like a LAVA flow of luxury.
story: Lavish. Farhan's cousin's wedding lasted five days. There were three thousand guests, a stage covered in roses, fireworks over the river, and seven kinds of biryani. Everyone agreed it was lavish: rich, elaborate and generous. As a verb, to lavish means to give generously, as when the grandmother lavished gold on the bride. The word comes from an old French word for a downpour of rain: generosity pouring down. Opposite: frugal. Synonyms: sumptuous, extravagant.

gre.s: Critics accused the company of hypocrisy: even as it cut workers' wages, it held a ____ banquet for its executives, complete with imported wine and live music.
gre.clue: complete with imported wine and live music

en: Looking or sounding sad and dismal
hook: LUGUBRIOUS: LUG-ubrious, LUGGING sadness around.
story: Lugubrious. Tanvir's old neighbour plays sad songs on his harmonium every evening. His face is long, his voice is slow and heavy, and even his jokes sound like funeral speeches. When he says good morning, it sounds like bad news. He is lugubrious: looking or sounding sad and dismal, often in an exaggerated way. The word comes from the Latin lugere, to mourn. Notice the long, slow, heavy sound of the word itself. Synonyms: mournful, doleful, gloomy.

gre.s: The director's films are relentlessly ____: long, slow scenes of grieving widows set to funeral music leave audiences longing for even a moment of levity.
gre.clue: long, slow scenes of grieving widows set to funeral music

en: Disturbing and horrifying because involving death or injury
hook: MACABRE: think 'MAKE A BURIAL' scene.
story: Macabre. The village storyteller loved to frighten children. His favourite tale was of a graveyard where skeletons danced at midnight and a headless boatman rowed coffins across the river. The children shivered but begged for more. His stories were macabre: disturbing and horrifying because they dwelt on death. The word recalls the Dance of Death, a medieval image of skeletons leading the living to the grave. Synonyms: grisly, gruesome, ghoulish.

gre.s: The museum's exhibit on the medieval plague was undeniably ____, displaying skulls, burial records, and paintings of corpses piled in the streets.
gre.clue: displaying skulls, burial records, and paintings of corpses piled in the streets

en: Sullen and gloomy
hook: MOROSE: MORE OF A ROSE losing its petals, wilting sadly.
story: Morose. After failing his driving test for the third time, Zayan came home, refused dinner, and sat on the balcony staring at the traffic. When his sister tried to cheer him up, he grunted and turned away. For two days he barely spoke. He was morose: sullen and gloomy. A morose person is not only sad but withdrawn and unwilling to talk. Contrast with lugubrious, which is sad in a showy, exaggerated way. Synonyms: sullen, glum, sulky.

gre.s: Although he had once been the life of every party, years of illness left him ____ and withdrawn, rarely speaking even to his oldest friends.
gre.clue: rarely speaking even to his oldest friends

en: Too eager to tell people what to do; intrusively interfering
hook: OFFICIOUS: acts like an OFFICER nobody appointed.
story: Officious. At a government office in Motijheel, one junior clerk would not let anyone pass without checking their forms, even people looking for the toilet. He corrected spelling on documents that were not his job, told visitors where to stand, and lectured an old man about his handwriting. He was officious: too eager to tell people what to do, intrusively interfering. Careful: officious does not mean official. Synonyms: meddlesome, bossy, intrusive.

gre.s: The ____ hall monitor, who had no real authority, nonetheless insisted on inspecting every student's bag and lecturing teachers about punctuality.
gre.clue: who had no real authority, nonetheless insisted on

en: A complex consequence of an action or event
hook: RAMIFICATION: branches (rami) spreading out from a decision.
story: Ramification. The government raised the price of diesel by twenty taka. It seemed a small change. But soon bus fares rose, then vegetable prices climbed because trucks cost more to run, and farmers could no longer afford to run their irrigation pumps. Each of these was a ramification: a complex, often unexpected consequence. Ramus is Latin for branch, so one decision branches out into many results. Synonyms: consequence, repercussion, implication.

gre.s: The committee hastily approved the plan without weighing a single ____ of its decision; within a year, unforeseen effects had rippled through every department.
gre.clue: unforeseen effects had rippled through every department

en: Calm, peaceful, and untroubled
hook: SERENE: SERENITY.
story: Serene. At five in the morning, Priya sat on the shore of Kaptai Lake. Mist hung over the green hills, the water lay perfectly still, and the only sound was a distant boatman's oar. After months of Dhaka traffic, she felt her whole body relax. The scene was serene: calm, peaceful and untroubled. A serene person stays calm even in a crisis. Serenity is the noun. Contrast with turbulent. Synonyms: tranquil, placid.

gre.s: In contrast to the frantic, crowded market just outside its walls, the monastery garden remained ____, its stillness broken only by birdsong.
gre.clue: its stillness broken only by birdsong

en: To replace, especially by force or scheming
hook: SUP-PLANT: uproot one PLANT and put another in its place.
story: Supplant. For decades the pedal rickshaw ruled Dhaka's narrow lanes. Then battery-powered auto-rickshaws arrived, faster and cheaper, and slowly pushed the old rickshaws off route after route. In some neighbourhoods they have supplanted them entirely: replaced them and taken their place. Supplant often suggests replacing by force or scheming. The Latin root means to trip someone up by the heel and then take their spot. Synonyms: replace, oust, displace.

gre.s: The ambitious deputy spent years flattering the board and quietly undermining his superior, plotting all the while to ____ her as head of the company.
gre.clue: quietly undermining his superior

en: Understood or implied without being stated
hook: TACIT: TACITURN, silent agreement.
story: Tacit. Mahin and his roommate share one small desk. Nobody ever discussed it, but Mahin uses it from seven to nine every evening, and his roommate takes over afterwards. They never quarrel about it. Their arrangement is tacit: understood without being stated. Tacit comes from the Latin for silent, the same root as taciturn, meaning a person of few words. Silence can signal tacit approval: by saying nothing, you agree. Synonyms: implicit, unspoken.

gre.s: Although the treaty never explicitly mentioned the disputed island, both nations had reached a ____ understanding that neither would station troops there.
gre.clue: never explicitly mentioned

en: To go beyond the limits of
hook: TRANS-CEND: climb (scend) ACROSS (trans) the limits.
story: Transcend. Lalon, the mystic singer of Kushtia, lived in a society divided by religion and caste. Yet his songs are sung by Hindus and Muslims, farmers and professors, rich and poor alike. His music transcends those divisions: it goes beyond their limits. Trans means beyond, and the rest comes from a Latin verb meaning to climb, as in ascend. To transcend is to climb beyond. Great art can transcend language and time. Synonyms: surpass, exceed, rise above.

gre.s: The finest translations ____ the limits of a word-for-word rendering; rather than merely copying sentences, they recreate the spirit of the original.
gre.clue: rather than merely copying sentences

en: A formal written work dealing systematically with a subject
hook: TREATISE: a book that TREATS a subject thoroughly.
story: Treatise. Anika's grandfather spent twenty years writing a five-hundred-page book on the rice varieties of Bengal. It has chapters on soil, history, climate and cooking, each carefully argued, with tables and footnotes. Agricultural scholars still cite it today. It is a treatise: a formal written work dealing systematically with a subject. Do not confuse it with treaty, an agreement between nations. Kautilya's Arthashastra is a famous ancient treatise on statecraft. Synonyms: monograph, dissertation.

gre.s: Far from being a casual collection of anecdotes, the book is a rigorous ____, methodically working through every aspect of the philosopher's theory of justice.
gre.clue: methodically working through every aspect
